identity.title: Starting, Progressing and Succeeding (academic skills pathway)
identity.practiceNoun: starting, progressing and succeeding at university
identity.agentDefinition: Starting, Progressing and Succeeding is one of thirteen academic skills pathways and the model's entry point: the dispositional layer of studying, from finding one's feet (the conventions of academic practice, mindset, motivation, goals, self-efficacy), through keeping going (sustaining motivation, handling setbacks and anxiety, seeking support early), to becoming a graduate (independence, graduate identity and capital, lifelong learning). Reach for it to place, sequence or assess a capability in the "why" and "who" of studying, or to translate one into its workplace form. It is not about the mechanics of managing one's learning (outcomes, criteria, feedback cycles, self-regulated learning phases), which belong to Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback.
identity.summary: The academic skills pathways model (2026) sets Starting, Progressing and Succeeding as the first of thirteen pathways and the programme's entry point, drawn from the opening and closing chapters of a study skills guide: on mindset, motivation and goals, and on becoming a graduate. It is the dispositional layer, who the student is becoming and why they are motivated, beside a companion pathway's mechanics of learning. It climbs in three tiers: starting (familiarising oneself with the conventions of academic practice, conforming to them and then expressing oneself within them, as amended by the model's author; what excelling means, the move from school or college to university, growth and fixed mindsets, mastery and performance motivation, goals and sub-goals, self-efficacy); progressing (sustaining motivation across a course, handling setbacks, disappointment and anxiety, realistic expectations without perfectionism, seeking support early); and succeeding (independence and self-direction, graduate identity, the move into professional life, lifelong learning). It rests on accounts of mindset, self-efficacy, achievement goals and graduate capital, which the guide cites. Its theory is Dweck, Bandura, Pintrich and Tomlinson; its main dispute is the weak evidence for growth mindset interventions (Part E).

tierProgression.masteryNote: This pathway lives in Marzano and Kendall's self-system more than any other: beliefs about one's own ability, motivation and emotional response. Across the tiers the weight moves from declarative knowledge of mindset and motivation, with a first recognition of one's own (Introductory), through procedures for sustaining goals and managing oneself under pressure (Intermediate), to self-direction and identity (Advanced). In Anderson and Krathwohl's terms it is metacognitive almost from the start, and the movement is from knowledge about oneself to acting on it unprompted. Mastery is becoming a graduate, the map's Advanced goal, which is the core's A11 ladder from compliance to flow.

theorySpine.overview:
- Three tiers, Introductory (starting), Intermediate (progressing) and Advanced (succeeding), each with a focus, content, a progression logic and links to other pathways (D:PTM, Pathway 1).
- Progression runs from finding one's feet, to sustaining and adapting, to becoming a graduate (D:PTM, Pathway 1).
- The pathway is the programme's entry point, surfaced first, introducing the others and carrying the orientation tone; every other pathway leans on it for the motivational and dispositional layer (D:PTM, Pathway 1).
- It is the dispositional layer, distinct from the mechanics of learning, whose self-regulated learning is its mechanical counterpart (D:PTM, Pathway 1).
- Tiers are anchored to experience of the practice, not to year of study (D:TSPEC, section 2).
- Across the tiers runs the evolution of the learner's self-identity as an academic practitioner: from learning and conforming to the conventions of academic practice, through expressing oneself within them and investing in one's development, to directing one's own practice independently; the pathway therefore carries metacognition (D-ing-0046).
theorySpine.corePrinciples:
- Success at university is subjective and has two sides: academic performance (marks, and the steps towards mastery of the discipline) and personal development (the attributes of graduate identity) (D:EAU, pp. 10-15).
- Excelling is exceeding expectations: achieving one's goals and more, and making tangible growth in competencies and behaviours (D:EAU, pp. 15-16).
- Finding success and excelling depend on three related factors: mindset, motivation and goals (D:EAU, p. 16).
- A growth mindset links effort to success and treats assessment and feedback as chances to develop; a fixed mindset treats ability as given (D:EAU, pp. 16-19, after Yeager and Dweck, 2012).
- Self-efficacy, belief in one's capacity to do what a task needs, underpins mindset, motivation and goals, and can be built through overcoming challenges, seeing peers succeed, positive feedback and managing stress and anxiety (D:EAU, pp. 19-21, after Bandura, 1977, 1994).
- Motivation is broadly towards performance (marks, comparison with others) or learning (mastery and personal development); it extends from mindset, rests on self-efficacy and on the value one places on a task, and fluctuates (D:EAU, pp. 21-23, after Dweck, 2012).
- Goals emerge from motivation; mastery goals serve learning and development better than targeted (performance) goals, and achievable goals sustain motivation (D:EAU, pp. 23-25, after Pintrich, 2005 and Zimmerman, Bandura and Martinez-Pons, 1992).
- Moving from the structured learning of school or college to directing one's own learning is one of the most significant challenges of the transition into higher education (D:EAU, p. 44).
- Becoming a graduate means building graduate capital in five related forms, human, social, cultural, identity and psychological, and being able to articulate it (D:EAU, pp. 247-251, after Tomlinson, 2017).
theorySpine.selection: Choose this pathway when the aim is a learner's disposition: what success means to them, their mindset, motivation, goals and confidence, keeping going, and seeing themselves as a graduate. For planning, monitoring and evaluating study, outcomes, criteria and feedback, choose `path:understanding-learning-assessment-feedback`; for reflection as a practice, `path:reflective-practice`; for learning on placement and professional identity in practice, `path:work-based-experiential-learning`; for exam anxiety and revision, `path:revising-exams`. It suits badly a learner who needs welfare or mental health support, which it can point to but not give.

analysis: **The guide's vocabulary against the benchmarks':** the guide says excelling, growth and fixed mindset, mastery and performance, self-efficacy, stress and anxiety, graduate identity, graduate capital, lifelong learner; the benchmarks say resilience, self-efficacy, self-management, independent learner, self-directed learning, employability. Both belong in the practice searcher's vocabulary for this pathway.
**Skill against theme:** two of the twelve extracts are skill. Dispositions appear in the benchmarks as attributes to list, not practices to describe.
**Book coverage:** Chapters 1, 2 and 14 carry all nine cards; academic voice (d3) is the least developed in the guide.

**Other authors:** META holds Pintrich (goal orientation) and Tinto (integration); the strand leads for mindset, self-efficacy, self-authorship and graduate capital are wanted (W-0050, W-0054, W-0063, W-0057).

gaps.coreOpenQuestions:
1. **P2 triggers:** 4 and 5: Bandura, Tomlinson, Kift, Sisk and others, the level descriptors and Vitae were read by summary only; Dweck, Pintrich, Yorke and Barnett only as the guide cites them (W-0050, W-0054 to W-0061, W-0031 to W-0034). The crosswalk is editorial.
2. **Levels:** `unknown` for every capability (D-ing-0001 (a)).
3. **Capability coverage:** settled (D-ing-0046, Abbott, 07:13). The four cards leave parts of every tier uncarded. Introductory: what success and excelling mean, and the move from school or college to university. Intermediate: seeking support early, handling setbacks and realistic expectations without perfectionism (`/02` covers stress and anxiety). Advanced: independence and self-direction, and lifelong learning (`/04` covers graduate capital only). Candidates for the model's author, temporary ids: c1 (Introductory) "Explain what success and excelling mean at university, in academic performance and personal development"; c2 (Intermediate) "Seek support early and from the right source when facing setbacks"; c3 (Advanced) "Direct one's own learning and development independently, as a lifelong learner". [Settled: Abbott did not take these candidates. Three capabilities added by the model's author, temporary ids: c1 (Introductory) "Recognise and follow the conventions of academic practice"; c2 (Intermediate) "Invest in strategic personal development as an academic practitioner"; c3 (Advanced) "Direct one's own academic practice, learning and development independently, as a lifelong learner". The Introductory tier is about familiarising oneself with academic conventions, conforming first and then expressing oneself within them, not explaining what success means; across the tiers runs the evolution of the learner's self-identity as an academic practitioner. Where expressing oneself within the conventions sits (c1, c2 or the tier text only) is ing's placement in the tier text, for Abbott to confirm.] [c2 reworded 08:04, D-ing-0048: "Develop an academic voice, and the confidence and sense of capability to own one's practice within its conventions" (was "Invest in strategic personal development as an academic practitioner"); the Intermediate tier is where the learner practitioner moves beyond conforming, an evolution in metacognitive awareness; expressing oneself within the conventions is carried here.]
4. **Key theory:** settled (D-ing-0047, Abbott, 07:13). The guide's two chapters rest on Dweck (mindset), Bandura (self-efficacy), Pintrich (goals) and Tomlinson (graduate capital); META holds Tinto (persistence) and Bridges (transition). None is ingested except Tinto, Bridges and Lave and Wenger. [Settled: the theory is Dweck (mindset), Bandura (self-efficacy), Pintrich (goals) and Tomlinson (graduate capital); Tinto, Bridges and the rest are supporting links. The four are queued at META's ing in that order.] [10:19: Pintrich is now a META run (2000; the guide cites 2005, not checked here).]
5. **The line with Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback:** the model puts disposition here and the mechanics there; the guide builds self-regulated learning on mindset, motivation and goals (p. 246), and goal setting is taught in both (here as mastery goals, there as the forethought phase).
12. **The line with the conventions pathways:** academic writing style and referencing conventions are taught in Academic Writing and Referencing; c1 here is the learner recognising academia's conventions as a whole and their own place within them, the start of an identity as an academic practitioner, and points to those pathways for the conventions themselves (D-ing-0046).
13. **Theory for the evolution beyond conforming:** settled (D-ing-0049, Abbott, 09:25). Abbott asks whether Biggs maps here. Biggs and Collis's SOLO taxonomy (1982) moves from quantitative levels (unistructural, multistructural: knowing more of the rules) to qualitative ones (relational, extended abstract: seeing how they fit and using them for one's own purpose); Biggs's declarative and functioning knowledge separates knowing about conventions from using them in one's own work. Both describe understanding, not voice or identity. Two fits for the identity side: Baxter Magolda's self-authorship (following external formulas, crossroads, self-authorship, internal foundation; after Kegan), which matches conforming, voice and self-direction across the three tiers; and Ivanič (1998) on writer identity and the self as author, for academic voice. None is yet ingested. [Settled (c): Baxter Magolda's self-authorship frames the evolution across the three tiers; SOLO (META's run) sits beside it for the understanding side; Ivanič for voice at Intermediate. Baxter Magolda and Ivanič queued at META's ing.]
6. **The line with Reflective Practice and Work-Based and Experiential Learning:** graduate identity is developed by reflecting on experience and through work-based learning (guide, pp. 248-249); this pathway owns graduate identity and capital, the others the practices that build them.
7. **The guide's coverage:** the transition from school or college has one paragraph (p. 44) and a sentence in Chapter 14 (p. 246); setbacks, help-seeking and perfectionism are touched only in passing (pp. 17-18, 22, 249); exam anxiety is in Chapter 13 (pp. 234-235), Revising and Exams' ground. The Intermediate tier will draw mostly on sources outside the guide (W-0062).
8. **The evidence on growth mindset:** the guide presents mindset as key; meta-analyses find weak average effects (A7a). A lesson can teach mindset with the strategies and support that make it work, and say what the evidence shows.
9. **Progression by level (A11):** drafted with the document (J-ing-0001; META D-0205; D-ing-0035, D-ing-0036, D-ing-0038, D-ing-0039). Every level was read by summary only; the entries are editorial readings of the descriptors and of the guide's sources.
10. **Templates:** proposed: a goal planner, a graduate capital audit and a success diary entry (the guide's own tasks).
11. **Source map:** what *Excelling at University* teaches for each capability is in its source map, not here.
14. **Vocabulary (D-ing-0050, Abbott, 11:10):** swept. The guide's glossary terms for this pathway are in B2a (and A4 where new); candidates from the model's tier text are in B2b; A10's direct terms are the term list v1.0 patterns as words, with the ruled second version's changes noted. The search patterns themselves are kept with each consuming project, not here. No published glossary of this pathway's vocabulary has yet been read; B2b stays candidates.
